A scathing report into the 2025 federal election has warned Australian democracy is “under assault” from increasingly aggressive third-party involvement, and called for stricter safeguards against domestic interference.

The Electoral Matters Committee handed down its interim report into conduct during last year’s election on Tuesday.

While Australians had “every reason to be proud of our electoral system”, in many contested electorates, the “carnival of our democracy was under attack,” Labor MP and committee chair Jerome Laxale said of the report.

“In recent years, the polarisation of the electorates and the growing threat of aggressive third party involvement has shaken the foundations of the voting process for polling place volunteers, electoral commission workers and, most importantly, voters,” Mr Laxale said.

The Bennelong MP said submissions warned of a “new normal if the experiences of 2025 are repeated, one where democracy would “head down the path of hyper-partisanship and institutionalised intimidation”.

“It is clear, through the evidence received so far, that any assault on democracy needs to be addressed,” he said.

“Voting is obligatory in Australia, as such there is a duty on the Commonwealth to make sure that every place of voting is inviting, safe and fit for purpose.

“Submissions about the 2025 election tell us that a line had been crossed, the conventions have been deliberately broken, and that the government needs to address it.”

In total, the committee made 14 recommendations, including increased accountability for behaviour at polling places and a legislated, enforceable code of conduct for candidates, campaign workers, third parties, and volunteers.

It recommended that the Australian Electoral Commission develop a registration system for polling booth campaigners, and that candidates, campaign workers, and third parties be required to formally register that they will comply with the code of conduct.

Further recommendations urged the government to review thresholds for significant third party and associated entities – formerly known as a political campaigner, whose fundraising exceeds $250,000 during the financial year.

Perhaps the most significant recommendation, however, was that the government introduce legislation to amend the authorisation framework to ensure voters know who political communications are coming from, including who is paying for communications if it is not the person or entity authorising the communications – as is a legal requirement.

The proposed reforms would also require that anyone participating in public debate be “accountable” for their communications, and that the AEC is empowered to enforce authorisation requirements.

The committee also recommended that the AEC review resourcing for pre-polling and pursue a majority of polling places be accessible.

More than 350 submissions were made to the inquiry.

In a statement, the committee said more evidence would be sought on the use of AI, consideration of fixed or extended terms of parliament, and on the size of parliament, before the final report is handed down in November.

Originally published as Election probes warns of ‘third party attack’, calls for transparency laws
